steps.explain: Complete the square to find the vertex.
Intercepts.
Draw the concave-up parabola through these points.

keyPoints.note: Complete the square for the vertex; solve y = 0 for the x-intercepts.

parts.hint: Reflect the negative part of y = x² − 2x − 4 up, then take reciprocals: zeros → asymptotes.

steps.explain: First take the absolute value: the part of the parabola below the \(x\)-axis (between \(1\pm\sqrt5\)) is reflected up, so the vertex becomes \((1,5)\).
Now take the reciprocal. Zeros of \(f\) become vertical asymptotes; large values become small (\(y\to0\) as \(x\to\pm\infty\)); the maximum 5 in the middle becomes a minimum \(\frac15\).
The whole graph is above the \(x\)-axis.

parts.answer: Take |f| (reflect the part below the x-axis), then the reciprocal: vertical asymptotes at \(x=1\pm\sqrt5\) (zeros of f), horizontal asymptote y = 0, local minimum \(\left(1,\frac15\right)\) from the vertex, y-intercept \(\frac14\); the graph is always positive, rising to infinity at both asymptotes.

keyPoints.note: Zeros of x² − 2x − 4 become vertical asymptotes; the turning value 5 becomes 1/5.

questions.stem:
The diagram shows the graph of \(y=f(x)\).

Draw sketches of the graphs of the following on separate number planes:

parts.hint: Keep the x ≥ 0 part and reflect it in the y-axis.

steps.explain: For \(x\ge0\), \(|x|=x\), so the graph is unchanged on the right of the \(y\)-axis.
For \(x\lt 0\), \(f(|x|)=f(-x)\): the right-hand half is reflected in the \(y\)-axis. The original left part (and \(x=-1\)) is thrown away.
Key features: \((0,1)\), zeros at \(x=\pm\frac12\), asymptote \(y=2\) on both sides.

parts.answer: Keep the part of y = f(x) for x ≥ 0 (through (0, 1), down to (1/2, 0), then up towards y = 2) and reflect it in the y-axis. The result is even: zeros at x = ±1/2, y-intercept 1, horizontal asymptote y = 2 on both sides; the part for x < 0 (including the asymptote x = −1) is discarded.

keyPoints.note: f(|x|) is even: copy the right-hand half onto the left.

parts.hint: y = ±√f(x): only where f ≥ 0; points with f = 0 or 1 stay put; y → ±√2.

steps.explain: \(y^2=f(x)\) means \(y=\pm\sqrt{f(x)}\). This only exists where \(f(x)\ge0\): for \(x\gt -1\). The branch for \(x\lt -1\) (where \(f\lt 0\)) disappears.
Invariant points: where \(f=0\) or \(f=1\), \(\sqrt f=f\). So \((\frac12,0)\) and \((0,1)\) stay; \((0,-1)\) is the mirror image.
Asymptotes: \(f\to2\) gives \(y\to\pm\sqrt2\); \(f\to\infty\) near \(x=-1\) keeps the vertical asymptote. Square-rooting lifts values between 0 and 1 and lowers values above 1.
Reflect the top half in the \(x\)-axis. At \((\frac12,0)\) the curve has a vertical tangent.

parts.answer: \(y=\pm\sqrt{f(x)}\), only where f(x) ≥ 0, i.e. for x > −1. Points where f = 0 or 1 stay fixed: (1/2, 0), (0, ±1). Asymptotes: x = −1 (both branches go to ±∞) and y = ±√2. The graph is symmetric about the x-axis and has vertical tangents at (1/2, 0). Nothing for x < −1.

keyPoints.note: Take ±√f(x) where f(x) ≥ 0. Asymptote y = 2 becomes y = ±√2.

questions.stem: The solution for the inequality \(\frac{3}{x-1}\lt 5\) can be expressed as:
questions.hint: Find x = 8/5 (equality) and x = 1 (undefined), then test each region or sketch.

steps.explain: Find where the two sides are equal and where the left side is undefined.
Sketch \(y=\frac{3}{x-1}\) and \(y=5\). The hyperbola is below the line for \(x\lt 1\) (where it is negative) and for \(x\gt\frac85\).
The inequality is strict and \(x=1\) is excluded, so both ends are open.
Multiplying both sides by \(x-1\) without care loses the \(x\lt 1\) part (options A, C).

keyPoints.note: Don't multiply by x − 1 (its sign is unknown). Use the critical values x = 1 and x = 8/5.

questions.stem: The graphs of \(y=ax\) and \(y=\tan^{-1}(bx)\) intersect at three distinct points if:
questions.hint: Compare the gradient of tan⁻¹(bx) at the origin (= b) with the gradient of the line (= a).

steps.explain: Both graphs pass through the origin, and both are odd functions, so other intersections come in a pair \(\pm x_0\).
Gradient of \(y=\tan^{-1}(bx)\) at the origin:

\(\tan^{-1}(bx)\) flattens out towards \(\pm\frac{\pi}{2}\), while the line keeps going. So there are two extra crossings only if the curve leaves the origin more steeply than the line, in the same direction: \(b\) and \(a\) have the same sign and \(|b|\gt|a|\).
Of the options only \(b\lt a\lt 0\) fits (option A, \(0\lt b\lt a\), has the line steeper — only one intersection).

keyPoints.note: The inverse-tan curve must start steeper than the line (|b| > |a|, same sign) so it can cross back.

questions.stem: The graph of the function \(y=\cos^{-1}(2x)\) is dilated horizontally by a dilation factor of 4 and then translated vertically by 3 units. What is its new equation?
questions.hint: Horizontal dilation factor k: x → x/k. Vertical translation: add outside the function.

steps.explain: A horizontal dilation by factor 4 replaces \(x\) by \(\frac{x}{4}\).
A vertical translation by 3 adds 3 to the whole function.
Multiplying \(x\) by 4 (option C) would compress the graph, not stretch it; adding 3 inside the brackets is a horizontal shift.

keyPoints.text: dilated horizontally by a dilation factor of 4
keyPoints.note: Replace x by x/4 (not 4x), then add 3 outside the inverse cosine.
